blocks.text: Nitrogen is a significant component of the air, known for its low reactivity because of its small size, symmetrical electron cloud and non-polar triple bond. With the configuration 1s2 2s2 2p3 nitrogen needs three electrons to complete its octet, so it forms a triple bond by sharing three electrons with another nitrogen atom (Figure 12.1). This bond has a bond enthalpy of +944 kJ mol-1, and the high energy needed to break it before new bonds can form makes N2 very unreactive. The second reason is the non-polarity of the bond: both atoms are the same, with zero electronegativity difference, so the three bonded pairs are shared equally.

blocks.long_description: Two nitrogen atoms share three pairs of electrons in a very strong, completely non-polar triple bond, so nitrogen gas hardly reacts and is used to blanket reactive materials. Ammonia, made from nitrogen and hydrogen by the Haber process, is pyramidal because of the lone pair on nitrogen; that lone pair accepts a proton from an acid, which makes ammonia a Bronsted-Lowry base and turns it into the tetrahedral ammonium ion with four identical bonds. In water the equilibrium with ammonium and hydroxide lies far to the left, so ammonia is a weak base. Heating an ammonium salt with a base reverses the process and drives off ammonia, the test for ammonium in salt analysis.
